<document source="specs/support-agent-tms-tool-contract/contracts/get-booking-status.md" type="spec" relevance="0.98" tokens="515">
## Input Schema

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "booking_reference": {"type": "string"}
  },
  "required": ["booking_reference"]
}
```

One required property: `booking_reference`. No customer id, no company id — scope is resolved from the authenticated session by the resolver of #18, never from a model-supplied argument.

**Pattern routing** (decided by the pattern of `booking_reference`, after trimming surrounding whitespace and upper-casing it, so `olt-2024-0001 ` routes as `OLT-2024-0001`): ([from plan](https://lore.gcp.re-cinq.com/repos/re-cinq/Otto/plans/b4b2026f-63ce-4f1a-80bb-7a971f01f47f#p_70b73bf0-839e-489b-bf55-3730d99be632), [from plan](https://lore.gcp.re-cinq.com/repos/re-cinq/Otto/plans/b4b2026f-63ce-4f1a-80bb-7a971f01f47f#p_912eac3d-6b9d-4909-b850-04ee4569dd5c))

| Pattern             | Route          | TMS endpoint                                        |
| ------------------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `^OLT-\d{4}-\d{4}$` | Order path     | `GET /orders/{idOrNumber}` (scope `orders:read`)    |
| `^SHP-\d{4}-\d{6}$` | Shipment path  | `GET /shipments/{idOrRef}` (scope `shipments:read`) |
| Anything else       | Not-found card | No TMS call                                         |

**Who may see a booking** (decided 2026-10-15). OLT's API names two customers on every order and shipment: `ordererCustomerNumber` booked it and `customerNumber` pays for it, often the same customer but not always (OLT's guide names a Netto booking paid by Salling). The booking is the signed-in customer's when the resolver's `customerNumber` is either one. On the order path the order decides for its shipments, which the published API returns without customer numbers; a shipment that does name a payer or orderer other than its order's means the TMS contradicts itself, and the tool escalates `customer_scope_conflict`. Anyone else's booking answers exactly as an unknown reference does. `defineTmsTool` requires this check from every TMS tool as its `ownership` option.
</document>
<document source="README.md" type="doc" relevance="0.96" tokens="1542">
## Configuration

Every setting is read from the environment at startup and fails loudly, by
name, when absent. `.env.example` lists all of them and contains no real value
and no model vendor credential.

Authentication is OpenID Connect with bearer tokens, and who signs customers in
is not settled (RD-5 in `specs/support-agent-tms-access`): the real login is
expected to be OLT's own Fast Track portal, pending KU-06. Until then the api
serves a stand-in for it, in `apps/api/src/dummyPortal/`: an OpenID Connect
provider at `OIDC_ISSUER` (`/api/oauth`), with a discovery document, its signing
keys, an authorization endpoint and a token endpoint. Choosing "Log ind" sends the
browser to the stand-in's Danish login page with a fresh state and a PKCE (S256)
challenge; a tester signs in there, the login redirects back with a code, and the
web app redeems it for a one-hour ES256 access token it keeps in memory only. The
token endpoint also takes the password grant (RFC 6749 §4.3), which the api tests
and the frame recorder use.

A successful login also opens a session on the stand-in, in an `HttpOnly` cookie
scoped to `/api/oauth`, so no script reads it and it never reaches `/api/ws`.
Ticking "Husk mig i 30 dage" keeps it for 30 days; otherwise the cookie ends with
the browser and the session after 12 hours. While it lives, the authorization
endpoint answers with a code at once, `prompt=none` answers `login_required`
instead of showing the page, and the code buys a refresh token as well, which
`grant_type=refresh_token` exchanges for a new access token and a new refresh
token. `/api/oauth/logout`, the discovery document's `end_session_endpoint`, ends
the session and every refresh token it granted. Taking a name off
`LOGIN_USERNAME` ends that tester's sessions at their next use; changing
`LOGIN_PASSWORD` does not, so to sign everyone out, delete the documents in
`loginSessions`.

The web app asks the login with `prompt=none` on every page load, so a reload
signs a tester straight back in while that session lives, and it shows its own
login screen only when the login answers `login_required`. It keeps the access
and refresh tokens in memory and renews the access token a minute before it
expires. Once no answer is running, it reopens the chat's socket on the same
conversation, since HAL Engine reads a token once per connection. A reconnect
after a dropped connection renews first, so the first one after an api restart
is accepted. "Log ud", at the foot of the sidebar, sends the browser to the
login's logout.

A tester signs in with a name from `LOGIN_USERNAME`, a comma-separated list of
lowercase names (letters, digits and hyphens, so one name alone must be lowercase
too, or the api refuses to start), all sharing `LOGIN_PASSWORD`. A typed name is
trimmed and lowercased before the check, so `Mette` logs in as `mette`. The name a
tester logs in under is the token's subject and so their user id, which keeps
each tester's conversations apart. The shared password makes this a way to tell
testers apart, not to keep one out of another's account, so no real customer data
may reach a deployment that uses it. A name may not equal `LOGIN_PASSWORD`, so a
Secret with its values swapped fails at startup. The name reaches HAL Engine's
connect log, the audit rows and the escalation webhook, so treat it as a tester's
personal data. `LOGIN_CUSTOMER_NUMBERS` maps names to the TMS customer each acts
for, as `name=customerNumber` pairs, and the token carries that number as
`customer_number`; a name with none can sign in but opens no connection.
`LOGIN_FIRST_CUSTOMER_NUMBER` instead gives every tester their own customer,
counting up from it in `LOGIN_USERNAME` order, so a new tester goes last or
moves everyone after them to another customer. Set one of the two, never both.

Otto verifies the token the way it will verify the real login's, in
`apps/api/src/oauth/customerIdentity.ts`: issuer, audience (`otto-web`), signature
and expiry, then one mapper turns the claims into a user and a customer number.
`discoverIdentitySource` already reads any provider's discovery document and keys,
and a test proves it reads the stand-in's. The WebSocket and HAL Engine's REST
chat routes accept only a token that verifies, sent as `Authorization: Bearer` or,
from a browser WebSocket, offered as the subprotocol; a connection that sends both
must send the same token in each. The connection carries the customer number as
its `workspaceId`. The signing key lives in api memory, so a restart invalidates
every token, but not the login's sessions: they live in MongoDB, so a browser with
a session or a refresh token gets a fresh token signed with the new key. When the real login arrives, the stand-in is deleted and Otto is
pointed at its issuer.

The TMS is reached with one server-held key, so it cannot tell customers apart,
and Otto enforces the customer boundary in two places.
`apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` alone decides which customer is asking: it
verifies the connection's own token again on each call, never the model's input.
Every TMS tool then checks that the answer is that customer's, through the
`ownership` check `defineTmsTool` requires: `get_booking_status` shows a booking
only to the customer who booked it or pays for it, and answers anyone else exactly
as it answers a reference that does not exist. No tool may declare a customer,
company or account id among its inputs, and only `toolAuth.ts` reads the
connection's headers; a TMS call gets the turn's user, session and deadline, never
its cookie, host or token.

`TMS_MODE` decides what the TMS tools reach. `stand-in`, where `recinq-test`
runs until OLT sends a key, answers made-up bookings of the made-up customers
from `apps/api/stand-in-tms`, never leaving the process; its README lists the
references, and anything else answers as OLT's API answers an unknown one.
`live` reaches `TMS_BASE_URL` (https) with `TMS_API_KEY`, which `config.ts` reads
once and the api sends as `x-api-key` on each request; the TMS client reads no
credential itself. In the chart that is `api.tmsMode`, `api.tmsBaseUrl` and the
Secret named by `api.tmsSecretName`, key `apiKey`.
</document>

## Sources

- The TMS API (`https://olt.dora-apps.com/api/ext/v1/openapi.json`) is operated by OLT (Dora Apps); the support agent and its tools are operated by re:cinq for OLT. ([from plan](https://lore.gcp.re-cinq.com/repos/re-cinq/Otto/plans/b4b2026f-63ce-4f1a-80bb-7a971f01f47f#p_38daa8d1-74b9-474c-8053-ce2a1fa0f952), [from plan](https://lore.gcp.re-cinq.com/repos/re-cinq/Otto/plans/b4b2026f-63ce-4f1a-80bb-7a971f01f47f#p_5bb355bf-3564-408a-b7b6-5c4eb520c89c))
- `api/tms-openapi.json` and `api/README.md`: the delivered API, and the `confirmed` set for the question map.
- The kick-off transcript's TMS screen-share (EDI reference, pickup and delivery windows, pallet counts, cold-chain class, proof of delivery, damage overview, delivery deltas, `P2T` split legs): the `hypothesis` set.
- The kick-off call: "if the agent can't answer, we will call the customer immediately."
- CFOAgent's Uniconta client: 1,381 lines, with mock mode swapping in a 333-line hand-written mock at the session layer, so the request builder, pagination and 401-relogin retry never run in mock mode.
- `the-expert`'s 30-second `TIMEOUT` is a whole-model-turn budget, not the number to copy for a single request.
- No HTTP-recording library (`msw`, `nock`, `polly`, `undici`'s `MockAgent`) is used anywhere in the org, so the harness specifies a format rather than adopting a tool.
- HAL Engine `chatOrchestrator.ts`: `for (round = 0; round <= maxToolRounds; round++)`; `:64-69`, `executeToolCalls` filling `sessionId` and `userId` from the session; `:191-193`, the `onError` path #138 makes unreachable for a crashed tool.
- HAL Engine `hal-engine/src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts:11-20`: `ToolContext` with `sessionId` and `userId`.
- HAL Engine `docs/adding-tool-evaluation.md`: `ToolEvalConfig`'s `{id, question, type, expectedCount}` shape and the session-sequence and bleed testing pattern the question map's row ids and parameter column bind to.
- CFOAgent `specs/017-ai-term-calculation/contracts/calculate-financial-term.md`: the per-tool contract shape, adopted unchanged.
- Lore memory: CFOAgent's `specs/009-evaluation-observability/spec.md` and `specs/018-llm-judge-scoring/spec.md` already treat a question-to-expected-tool set as the unit of agent evaluation. No prior decision found for a third-party API client with a replaceable transport seam, a fixture format beyond CFOAgent's hand-typed golden-test fixtures, tool-authoring conventions, or FAQ-to-endpoint mapping (`lore-gaps.md` G4, G33, G35, G48, G50, G51).

## Out of Scope
</document>

<document source="apps/api/src/oauth/customerIdentity.ts" type="code" relevance="1.00" tokens="99">
// The one place a token's claims become Otto's identity; a user with no customer company is no identity at all.
export function identityFromClaims(claims: JWTPayload): CustomerIdentity | null {
  const customerNumber = claims[CUSTOMER_NUMBER_CLAIM];
  if (!claims.sub || typeof customerNumber !== 'string' || customerNumber === '') return null;
  return {userId: claims.sub, customerNumber};
}
</document>
<document source="apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts" type="code" relevance="0.95" tokens="129">
// FR-034: the customer comes from the login, so a tool that asks the model for one is refused before it can register.
export function enforceNoCustomerInput({name, inputSchema}: ToolDefinition): void {
  const declared = propertyNamesOf(inputSchema).find((property) =>
    CUSTOMER_IDENTIFIER.test(wordsOf(property))
  );
  if (declared !== undefined) {
    throw new Error(
      `Tool ${name} declares ${declared} in its inputSchema; the customer comes from the login, never from the model (FR-034).`
    );
  }
}
</document>

<section name="Architecture Decisions" source="adrs" priority="2">
<document source="adrs/ADR-001-tms-authentication.md" type="adr" relevance="1.00" tokens="1310">
## Context

The kick-off transcript named three options for how a customer's identity reaches the TMS. The delivered OLT TMS External API removes two of them. It authenticates with a single `x-api-key` header on every request; there is no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. This was confirmed by the API guide (`api/README.md`) and the OpenAPI spec (`api/tms-openapi.json`, `components.schemas` is empty, `securitySchemes` declares only `ApiKeyAuth`). OLT issues and manages the key; re:cinq receives one and stores it in `TMS_API_KEY`.

### Customer identity to us

Who signs the customer in is open (RD-5 in `specs/support-agent-tms-access`). Whichever provider does, the authenticated identity names a user and the customer company they act for, and that company carries a TMS `customerNumber`. The resolver reads that number from the verified token on every tool call.

The stand-in login (`apps/api/src/dummyPortal/`) is an OpenID Connect provider whose access tokens carry the `customer_number` claim (`apps/api/src/oauth/customerIdentity.ts:CUSTOMER_NUMBER_CLAIM`). When the real login lands, only the claim name and the provider's discovery URL change; the resolver interface is unchanged.

### Where `customerNumber` lives

CFOAgent's shipped pattern for per-user credentials stores data in the Clerk organisation's `privateMetadata`, encrypted with `encryptField` (`re-cinq/CFOAgent lib/services/clerk.ts`, `encryption.ts`, `uniconta-session-cache.ts`). Note: CFOAgent's own architecture docs describe Secret Manager and Firestore; the code uses Clerk `privateMetadata`. This ADR cites the code, not the docs.

For Otto, the `customerNumber` rides in the access token as the `customer_number` claim (see `customerIdentity.ts`). The stand-in login writes it there; the real login is expected to do the same (RD-5). The customer company's number is not stored separately in Clerk metadata for this agent — the JWT claim is sufficient, because the stand-in's tokens are short-lived and re:cinq never persists them.

A customer mapped to the wrong `customerNumber` by the identity provider is a breach with no error message: the tool will answer with data from another customer's bookings without any indication that anything is wrong. The mapping must be verified against OLT's customer list before a live deployment.

### No active organisation

`authenticateWebSocket` returns `null` for any token that does not verify or does not carry a customer number. HAL Engine refuses the WebSocket upgrade when `auth.ws` returns `null`. The customer receives the WebSocket close code, not an application-level message. An HTTP response with a Danish `400` on the login redirect is returned by the stand-in login for a user mapped to no customer company (`apps/api/src/dummyPortal/` — token issued but connection refused at the WebSocket level).

The ticket requires a Danish refusal at both the HTTP route and the WebSocket upgrade. The WebSocket refusal is implemented (return `null` from `auth.ws`). The HTTP route's Danish message for the no-customer case is an **open condition**: the stand-in login's error message at that step has not been reviewed by a Danish speaker. See `KU-15` and `docs/danish-review.md`.

### Clerk org roles

OLT's customers create their own portal users with different roles (kick-off 2026-08-17). The TMS key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so a user's role cannot narrow what the TMS returns — the key is the same for every user in the company. Role-based narrowing of results must happen in the support agent's own code if required. This pilot is read-only booking questions; no further narrowing is applied in the PoC.

## Decision

**Option C is accepted**: Otto holds one global server-side TMS API key (`TMS_API_KEY`), and the customer boundary is enforced entirely in our code. Options A and B are rejected (reasons below).

**The customer identifier is never a model-supplied tool input.** Under all three options, the `customerNumber` used in a TMS call is derived server-side from the authenticated identity, never from a value the model chose or the caller supplied. Under Option C this rule is the only barrier between two customers: a tool that accepts a customer identifier from the model bypasses it entirely, which is a breach and not a bug. `registerTools` refuses any tool definition that declares a customer, company or account identifier in its `inputSchema` at any depth (FR-034), and a test walks every registered tool in the api to confirm none do (`apps/api/test/customerBoundary.test.ts`).

The single code path where filtering happens is `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts`, exported as `createCustomerScopeResolver`. Every TMS tool reaches the TMS exclusively through this resolver; `registerTools` is the enforcement point. A tool that bypasses `toolAuth.ts` is a breach and not a bug.

The test that proves customer B's booking id returns an authorization error rather than data:
`apps/api/test/bookingStatusPaths.test.ts` — `shows $reference paid for by $payer and booked by $orderer: $shown` (shown=false when neither payer nor orderer matches the resolver's customer) and `answers customer 20002's shipment exactly as a reference that exists for nobody`.
</document>
</section>

// The one place a token's claims become Otto's identity; a user with no customer company is no identity at all.
export function identityFromClaims(claims: JWTPayload): CustomerIdentity | null {
  const customerNumber = claims[CUSTOMER_NUMBER_CLAIM];
  if (!claims.sub || typeof customerNumber !== 'string' || customerNumber === '') return null;
  return {userId: claims.sub, customerNumber};
}

// FR-034: the customer comes from the login, so a tool that asks the model for one is refused before it can register.
export function enforceNoCustomerInput({name, inputSchema}: ToolDefinition): void {
  const declared = propertyNamesOf(inputSchema).find((property) =>
    CUSTOMER_IDENTIFIER.test(wordsOf(property))
  );
  if (declared !== undefined) {
    throw new Error(
      `Tool ${name} declares ${declared} in its inputSchema; the customer comes from the login, never from the model (FR-034).`
    );
  }
}

<document source="adrs/ADR-001-tms-authentication.md" type="adr" relevance="1.00" tokens="1310">
## Context

The kick-off transcript named three options for how a customer's identity reaches the TMS. The delivered OLT TMS External API removes two of them. It authenticates with a single `x-api-key` header on every request; there is no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. This was confirmed by the API guide (`api/README.md`) and the OpenAPI spec (`api/tms-openapi.json`, `components.schemas` is empty, `securitySchemes` declares only `ApiKeyAuth`). OLT issues and manages the key; re:cinq receives one and stores it in `TMS_API_KEY`.

### Customer identity to us

Who signs the customer in is open (RD-5 in `specs/support-agent-tms-access`). Whichever provider does, the authenticated identity names a user and the customer company they act for, and that company carries a TMS `customerNumber`. The resolver reads that number from the verified token on every tool call.

The stand-in login (`apps/api/src/dummyPortal/`) is an OpenID Connect provider whose access tokens carry the `customer_number` claim (`apps/api/src/oauth/customerIdentity.ts:CUSTOMER_NUMBER_CLAIM`). When the real login lands, only the claim name and the provider's discovery URL change; the resolver interface is unchanged.

### Where `customerNumber` lives

CFOAgent's shipped pattern for per-user credentials stores data in the Clerk organisation's `privateMetadata`, encrypted with `encryptField` (`re-cinq/CFOAgent lib/services/clerk.ts`, `encryption.ts`, `uniconta-session-cache.ts`). Note: CFOAgent's own architecture docs describe Secret Manager and Firestore; the code uses Clerk `privateMetadata`. This ADR cites the code, not the docs.

For Otto, the `customerNumber` rides in the access token as the `customer_number` claim (see `customerIdentity.ts`). The stand-in login writes it there; the real login is expected to do the same (RD-5). The customer company's number is not stored separately in Clerk metadata for this agent — the JWT claim is sufficient, because the stand-in's tokens are short-lived and re:cinq never persists them.

A customer mapped to the wrong `customerNumber` by the identity provider is a breach with no error message: the tool will answer with data from another customer's bookings without any indication that anything is wrong. The mapping must be verified against OLT's customer list before a live deployment.

### No active organisation

`authenticateWebSocket` returns `null` for any token that does not verify or does not carry a customer number. HAL Engine refuses the WebSocket upgrade when `auth.ws` returns `null`. The customer receives the WebSocket close code, not an application-level message. An HTTP response with a Danish `400` on the login redirect is returned by the stand-in login for a user mapped to no customer company (`apps/api/src/dummyPortal/` — token issued but connection refused at the WebSocket level).

The ticket requires a Danish refusal at both the HTTP route and the WebSocket upgrade. The WebSocket refusal is implemented (return `null` from `auth.ws`). The HTTP route's Danish message for the no-customer case is an **open condition**: the stand-in login's error message at that step has not been reviewed by a Danish speaker. See `KU-15` and `docs/danish-review.md`.

### Clerk org roles

OLT's customers create their own portal users with different roles (kick-off 2026-08-17). The TMS key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so a user's role cannot narrow what the TMS returns — the key is the same for every user in the company. Role-based narrowing of results must happen in the support agent's own code if required. This pilot is read-only booking questions; no further narrowing is applied in the PoC.

## Decision

**Option C is accepted**: Otto holds one global server-side TMS API key (`TMS_API_KEY`), and the customer boundary is enforced entirely in our code. Options A and B are rejected (reasons below).

**The customer identifier is never a model-supplied tool input.** Under all three options, the `customerNumber` used in a TMS call is derived server-side from the authenticated identity, never from a value the model chose or the caller supplied. Under Option C this rule is the only barrier between two customers: a tool that accepts a customer identifier from the model bypasses it entirely, which is a breach and not a bug. `registerTools` refuses any tool definition that declares a customer, company or account identifier in its `inputSchema` at any depth (FR-034), and a test walks every registered tool in the api to confirm none do (`apps/api/test/customerBoundary.test.ts`).

The single code path where filtering happens is `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts`, exported as `createCustomerScopeResolver`. Every TMS tool reaches the TMS exclusively through this resolver; `registerTools` is the enforcement point. A tool that bypasses `toolAuth.ts` is a breach and not a bug.

The test that proves customer B's booking id returns an authorization error rather than data:
`apps/api/test/bookingStatusPaths.test.ts` — `shows $reference paid for by $payer and booked by $orderer: $shown` (shown=false when neither payer nor orderer matches the resolver's customer) and `answers customer 20002's shipment exactly as a reference that exists for nobody`.
